chunks: "Conceptually, voltage is the push and current is the flow.
When I put a voltage across a resistor, it creates an electric field inside it, and that field pushes on the free electrons.
Resistance is how hard the material makes it for them to move. The reason the relationship is linear is collisions.
Electrons don't just accelerate forever; they keep bumping into vibrating atoms and impurities, so they reach an average drift speed that's proportional to the field.
Twice the voltage means twice the field, twice the drift speed, and twice the current. That's Ohm's law.
The water analogy captures it nicely: voltage is pressure, current is flow rate, and the resistor is a narrow section of pipe.
A longer or narrower pipe restricts flow more, the same way a longer, thinner wire has more resistance. Two consequences fall out of this picture.
Those collisions turn electrical energy into heat, which is why resistors get warm, I to the 2R .
And if the material gets hotter, atoms vibrate more and electrons collide more often, so a metal's resistance goes up with temperature."
